specStatements.text: A lens forms an image by refracting light. In a convex lens, parallel rays of light are brought to a focus at the principal focus. The distance from the lens to the principal focus is called the focal length. Ray diagrams are used to show the formation of images by convex and concave lenses.
The image produced by a convex lens can be either real or virtual. The image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.
Students should be able to construct ray diagrams to illustrate the similarities and differences between convex and concave lenses.
The magnification produced by a lens can be calculated using the equation:
Magnification is a ratio and so has no units.
Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm.

A concave lens will be represented by:

scopeNotes.statement: Magnification is a ratio and so has no units.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every magnification in this material is written as a bare number — 3, 0.30, 2.5 — and never carries mm, cm or any other unit. Where an option attaches a unit to a magnification it is always a distractor, and its rationale says that dividing a height by a height cancels the unit. No item asks for a unit of magnification and no correct option supplies one.

scopeNotes.statement: Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: All heights are quoted in mm or in cm and in no other unit. Where a question deliberately mixes the two, the correct response is to convert so that both heights use the same unit; metres are never required, and an option that converts to metres is marked as a distractor.

The equation is quoted in the specification's own form, image height over object height, in the concept entry and in every rationale that uses it. The inverted form is never presented as correct, and no rearranged or extended version of the equation is required of students.

concepts.definition: A shaped piece of transparent material that forms an image by refracting light. The light changes direction as it enters the lens and again as it leaves, and that bending is what forms the image.
A lens that is thicker in the middle than at its edges. Rays of light arriving parallel to the principal axis are brought together to a focus at the principal focus.

A lens that is thinner in the middle than at its edges. Rays arriving parallel to the principal axis are spread apart, so that after the lens they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the object.
The straight line through the centre of the lens, at right angles to it, used as the reference line in every ray diagram.

The point on the principal axis at which rays of light that arrive parallel to that axis are brought to a focus by a convex lens. For a concave lens it is the point from which those rays appear to spread out.
The distance from the lens to the principal focus. It is a fixed property of a given lens: moving the object or the screen does not change it.
A drawing that uses straight lines with arrows to show the paths of selected rays of light, used to show how a lens forms an image and how large that image is.
An image formed where rays of light actually meet. Because the light really arrives there, a real image can be caught on a screen placed at that position.
An image formed where rays of light only appear to come from. The rays do not actually meet there, so no screen can catch it, but it can be seen by looking through the lens.

concepts.term: Image produced by a convex lens
concepts.definition: It can be either real or virtual. With the object further from the lens than the principal focus the image is real and inverted; with the object nearer than the principal focus the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

concepts.term: Image produced by a concave lens
concepts.definition: It is always virtual. Wherever the object is placed, the image is upright, smaller than the object and on the same side of the lens as the object.

concepts.term: Constructing a convex lens ray diagram
concepts.definition: Two rays are enough. A ray from the top of the object parallel to the principal axis is refracted through the principal focus beyond the lens; a ray through the centre of the lens carries straight on. The top of the image is where they cross.

concepts.term: Constructing a concave lens ray diagram
concepts.definition: A ray from the top of the object parallel to the principal axis is refracted so that it appears to come from the principal focus on the object side; a ray through the centre carries straight on. The image is found where the lines traced back cross.

How many times larger the image is than the object, calculated using magnification = (image height)/(object height). A value greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; a value less than 1 means it is smaller.
Magnification is a ratio of two lengths, so the unit on the top cancels the unit on the bottom and the answer is a plain number with no unit attached.

concepts.term: Measuring image height and object height
concepts.definition: Both heights should be measured in either mm or cm, and both must be in the same unit before they are divided, otherwise the ratio obtained is wrong.
In ray diagrams a convex lens is drawn as a vertical straight line with an arrowhead at each end pointing outwards, away from the principal axis.
In ray diagrams a concave lens is drawn as a vertical straight line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards, towards the principal axis.

misconceptions.question: Does a lens make an image in the same way as a mirror?
misconceptions.correct: A lens forms an image by refracting light: the light passes through the lens and is bent.
misconceptions.misconception: A lens bounces light off its shiny surface to make an image, just as a mirror does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lenses and mirrors are taught in the same topic, both are smooth and shiny, and both give images described as real or virtual, so the mechanism learned for mirrors is transferred to the lens.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: a lens forms an image by refracting light. The light goes through the lens and changes direction at each surface. A little light does reflect from the surfaces, but that is not how the image is made.

misconceptions.question: Is the focal length the distance from the lens to the image?
misconceptions.correct: The focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus.
misconceptions.misconception: The focal length is however far the image happens to be from the lens, so it changes when the object is moved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In practical work students measure the lens-to-screen distance when the image is sharp, and for a very distant object that distance really is the focal length, so the special case is remembered as the definition.
misconceptions.correction: The principal focus is where rays that arrive parallel to the principal axis are brought to a focus. The focal length is the fixed distance from the lens to that point, and it does not change when the object is moved.

misconceptions.question: Does the image always form at the principal focus?
misconceptions.correct: The image forms where the rays from the object meet, which is generally not at the principal focus.
misconceptions.misconception: The lens focuses light at the principal focus, so that is where the image must appear.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word focus is used both for the special point and for a sharp image, and the only ray diagram many students remember is the one for a very distant object, where the image really does form at the principal focus.
misconceptions.correction: The principal focus only tells you where rays parallel to the axis are brought together. Rays from a nearby object are not parallel, so they cross somewhere else, and that is where the image forms.

misconceptions.question: Does light bend only once when it goes through a lens?
misconceptions.correct: The light refracts as it enters the lens and refracts again as it leaves it.
misconceptions.misconception: The light travels straight through the glass and is bent only at the surface where it comes out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ray diagrams draw a single bend at the lens line for simplicity, and refraction is often first taught with one boundary, so a second change of direction is not expected.
misconceptions.correction: A lens has two surfaces and the light is refracted at both. The single bend drawn at the lens line in a ray diagram is a shorthand for the two refractions that actually take place.

misconceptions.question: Can a concave lens ever produce a real image?
misconceptions.correct: No. The image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.
misconceptions.misconception: If the object is far enough away, a concave lens will bring the light together and make a real image on a screen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a convex lens gives a real image of a distant object and assume the same rule applies to any lens once the object is far enough away.
misconceptions.correction: A concave lens spreads light out, so the rays leaving it never meet. They only appear to come from a point on the object side, so the image is always virtual and can never be caught on a screen.

misconceptions.question: Does virtual mean that the image cannot be seen?
misconceptions.correct: A virtual image can be seen by looking through the lens; it simply cannot be caught on a screen.
misconceptions.misconception: A virtual image is one that cannot be seen at all, so any image you can actually look at must be real.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech virtual suggests something not really there, so students read it as invisible rather than as a statement about where the rays actually go.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual describes the rays, not the viewer. The rays only appear to come from the image position, so no screen catches it, but the eye can still see it by looking through the lens.

misconceptions.question: Does a convex lens always give a real, inverted image?
misconceptions.correct: No. The image produced by a convex lens can be either real or virtual.
misconceptions.misconception: A convex lens always turns the picture upside down and always gives an image you could catch on a screen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearly all classroom work with a convex lens uses an object beyond the principal focus, which does give a real inverted image, so that case is taken to be the only one.
misconceptions.correction: When the object is closer to the lens than the principal focus, the rays leaving the lens are still spreading out and the image is virtual, upright and magnified, as in a magnifying glass.

misconceptions.question: Is the image from a concave lens upside down?
misconceptions.correct: No. A concave lens always gives an upright image.
misconceptions.misconception: The image from a concave lens is inverted, because lenses turn images over.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first image a student meets is the real inverted image from a convex lens, and inversion becomes attached to the idea of a lens rather than to that particular case.
misconceptions.correction: Rays through a concave lens are spread out and traced back to a point above the axis on the object side, so the image comes out upright, smaller and virtual every time.

misconceptions.question: Is the ray through the centre of the lens bent?
misconceptions.correct: No. In a ray diagram the ray through the centre of the lens is drawn straight on.
misconceptions.misconception: Every ray that meets a lens is bent once, at the middle of the lens, so even the central ray is drawn bending there and through the principal focus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a lens refracts light and apply that to all rays equally, without noticing that the two surfaces are parallel at the centre so the direction is unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: At the centre the two faces of the lens are effectively parallel, so a ray passing through there emerges travelling in its original direction. It is drawn as a straight line through the centre.

misconceptions.question: Where does the parallel ray go after a concave lens?
misconceptions.correct: It is refracted outwards, so that it appears to have come from the principal focus on the object side.
misconceptions.misconception: The parallel ray passes through the principal focus on the far side of the lens, exactly as it does for a convex lens.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The convex rule is learned first and is applied to the concave diagram without change, because both lenses are drawn with a principal focus marked.
misconceptions.correction: A concave lens diverges the light. The refracted ray travels away from the axis, and only the dashed line traced backwards passes through the principal focus, which lies on the object side.

misconceptions.question: Should a magnification be given a unit?
misconceptions.correct: No. Magnification is a ratio and so has no units.
misconceptions.misconception: The heights were measured in centimetres, so the magnification must be in centimetres too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are trained to carry a unit through every calculation and to lose marks for leaving one out, so they attach the unit of the measurements they started with.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing a height by a height cancels the unit: cm divided by cm leaves a plain number. A magnification is written as a bare number such as 3 or 0.30.

misconceptions.question: Which way round is the magnification equation?
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification is the object height divided by the image height, because you start with the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The object comes first in the story of what happens, and in the phrase object and image, so it is put first in the fraction as well.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives magnification = (image height)/(object height). The image height goes on top, so an image larger than the object gives a magnification greater than 1.

misconceptions.question: Can heights in mm and cm be divided as they stand?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both heights must be in the same unit before they are divided.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification has no units anyway, so it does not matter if one height is in cm and the other in mm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that magnification has no unit is remembered as meaning that units do not matter anywhere in the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: The unit only cancels if it is the same on the top and the bottom. Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm, so convert one of them first.

misconceptions.question: Must a magnification be greater than 1?
misconceptions.correct: No. A magnification less than 1 means the image is smaller than the object.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification means making something bigger, so the answer must always come out greater than 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of magnify is to enlarge, so an answer such as 0.30 looks like a mistake and gets turned upside down to give 3.3.
misconceptions.correction: In physics magnification is just the ratio of image height to object height. If the image is smaller the ratio is less than 1, and that is the correct answer.

misconceptions.question: Which lens symbol has arrowheads pointing inwards?
misconceptions.correct: Inward-pointing arrowheads represent a concave lens; outward-pointing arrowheads represent a convex lens.
misconceptions.misconception: Inward arrowheads mean a convex lens, because a convex lens brings the rays inwards to a focus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students try to make the symbol describe what the lens does to light rather than remembering that it records the shape of the lens.
misconceptions.correction: The arrowheads follow the shape, not the action. A convex lens bulges outwards, so its arrowheads point outwards; a concave lens is hollowed inwards, so its arrowheads point inwards.

misconceptions.question: Should a ray diagram show the true curved shape of the lens?
misconceptions.correct: No. The lens is drawn as a single vertical line with arrowheads at its ends.
misconceptions.misconception: A ray diagram should show the lens as it really looks, curved on both faces, with the rays bending at each curved surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are told the lens works because of its curved surfaces, so they assume the diagram must show them, and textbook photographs reinforce the picture.
misconceptions.correction: In ray diagrams the lens is represented by a straight line with arrowheads, and all the bending is drawn happening at that line. The symbol records the type of lens, not its true shape.

misconceptions.question: Is a virtual image always smaller than the object?
misconceptions.correct: No. A convex lens can form a virtual image that is larger than the object.
misconceptions.misconception: Virtual means the image is not properly there, so it is always a small, faint copy of the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The virtual image students meet most often is the diminished one from a concave lens, and the word virtual suggests something weaker than the real thing.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual says only that the rays appear to come from the image. A magnifying glass gives a virtual image that is upright and larger than the object.

misconceptions.question: Does an upright image mean the image is real?
misconceptions.correct: No. An upright image formed by a lens is virtual; a real image from a lens is inverted.
misconceptions.misconception: If the image looks the same way up as the object then it must be the real one, because that is how the object really looks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Real is heard as meaning true to life, so an image that looks correct is called real and an upside-down one is called false.
misconceptions.correction: Real and virtual describe whether the rays actually meet, not how the image looks. Whether it can be caught on a screen is the test, and a real image from a lens comes out inverted.

mcqs.stem: Rays of light travelling parallel to the principal axis pass into a convex lens. What happens to these rays?

options.text: They are refracted and brought to a focus at the principal focus
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: in a convex lens, parallel rays of light are brought to a focus at the principal focus.

options.text: They are reflected from the front face of the lens to a point
options.rationale: A student who thinks a lens behaves like a mirror expects the light to bounce off the surface instead of passing through the lens.

options.text: They are refracted and cross each other at the focal length
options.rationale: This confuses a distance with a place: the focal length is how far the principal focus is from the lens, not a point where rays meet.

options.text: They pass straight through and bend only as they leave
options.rationale: Reflects m04: light travels straight through the glass and is bent only at the exit surface, so it is never brought to a focus by refraction.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the focal length of a convex lens?

options.text: The distance from the lens to the object being viewed
options.rationale: This makes the focal length depend on where the object is put, when in fact it is a fixed property of the lens itself.

options.text: The distance from the lens to the principal focus
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: the distance from the lens to the principal focus is called the focal length.

options.text: The distance from the lens to the sharp image
options.rationale: The lens-to-screen distance equals the focal length only for a very distant object; moving the object changes it, so it cannot be the definition.

options.text: The thickness of the lens where it is widest
options.rationale: A student who pictures the real curved lens rather than its optical behaviour links focal length to the physical shape of the glass.

mcqs.stem: A convex lens forms an image of a distant tree on a screen. Where does the light change direction?

options.text: Only at the surface where the light leaves the lens
options.rationale: Ray diagrams show one bend for simplicity, so students often think only the exit surface refracts the light.

options.text: At the shiny front face, where light is reflected
options.rationale: This treats the lens as a mirror; a little light does reflect, but the image is formed by refraction through the lens.

options.text: As it enters the lens and again as it leaves
options.rationale: A lens has two surfaces and refraction happens at both, which together bring the parallel rays from the tree to a focus.

options.text: Only at the middle, where it is thickest
options.rationale: The centre of the lens is exactly where a ray is not deviated, so this reverses what actually happens there.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the image formed by a concave lens is always true?

options.text: It is real if the object is far enough away
options.rationale: This carries the convex lens rule across; a concave lens spreads light out, so its rays never actually meet.

options.text: It is inverted, like the image from a lens
options.rationale: Inversion belongs to the real image from a convex lens; a concave lens always gives an upright image.

options.text: It is too faint for anyone to look at it
options.rationale: Virtual is misread as invisible; the image can be seen perfectly well by looking through the lens.

options.text: It is virtual, wherever the object is
options.rationale: The specification states that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual, whatever the object distance.

mcqs.stem: An object is placed between a convex lens and its principal focus, as in a magnifying glass. What sort of image is formed?

options.text: A real image, inverted and larger than the object
options.rationale: This applies the familiar case of an object beyond the principal focus to a situation where it does not hold.

options.text: A virtual image, upright and larger than the object
options.rationale: Inside the principal focus the rays leaving the lens are still diverging, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

options.text: A virtual image, upright but smaller than it
options.rationale: The image is indeed virtual, but a student who thinks virtual images must be diminished picks the wrong size.

options.text: A real image formed at the principal focus
options.rationale: The principal focus only fixes where parallel rays meet; it is not where the image of every object appears.

mcqs.stem: How can you tell that an image formed by a lens is real rather than virtual?

options.text: It appears the same way up as the object does
options.rationale: Real is heard as true to life, but a real image formed by a lens is in fact inverted.

options.text: It can be seen by looking through the lens
options.rationale: Virtual images are seen this way too, so being visible does not distinguish a real image from a virtual one.

options.text: It can be caught on a screen put where it forms
options.rationale: A real image is formed where rays of light actually meet, so a screen placed there shows it.

options.text: It is on the same side of the lens as the object
options.rationale: This describes where a virtual image sits; a real image from a lens forms on the far side.

mcqs.stem: In a ray diagram for a convex lens, how is the ray from the top of the object to the centre of the lens drawn?

options.text: It is bent so that it passes through the principal focus
options.rationale: This applies the rule for the parallel ray to the central ray, on the assumption that every ray must be bent.

options.text: It is curved to follow the two faces of the lens
options.rationale: Rays are always drawn as straight lines, and the lens itself is drawn as a straight line in ray diagrams.

options.text: It is bent back to run parallel to the principal axis
options.rationale: This reverses the parallel-ray rule and applies it to the wrong ray altogether.

options.text: It carries straight on, with no change of direction
options.rationale: At the centre the faces of the lens are effectively parallel, so the ray emerges travelling in its original direction.

mcqs.stem: In a ray diagram for a concave lens, a ray arrives parallel to the principal axis. How is it drawn after the lens?

options.text: Spreading away from the principal axis
options.rationale: A concave lens diverges the light, and only the line traced backwards passes through the principal focus.

options.text: Bending in to reach the principal focus beyond
options.rationale: This uses the convex lens rule unchanged, which is the commonest error in concave lens diagrams.

options.text: Carrying straight on to the far side of it
options.rationale: Only the ray through the centre of the lens is undeviated; a parallel ray away from the centre is refracted.

options.text: Bending inwards to cross the principal axis
options.rationale: Rays that cross would give a real image, which a concave lens can never produce.

mcqs.stem: A student draws ray diagrams for a convex lens and for a concave lens, using the same object in each. Which feature is the same in both diagrams?

options.text: Both images are turned upside down compared with the object
options.rationale: Reflects m08: lenses always turn images over, so both the convex and concave images are inverted, making inversion the shared feature.

options.text: Both images can be caught on a screen behind
options.rationale: Only a real image can be caught on a screen, and a concave lens never forms one.

options.text: The ray through the centre of the lens is undeviated
options.rationale: This construction rule is shared by both lenses, and is one of the similarities a comparison of the diagrams should bring out.

options.text: The parallel ray goes to the focus beyond the lens
options.rationale: That happens for the convex lens only; for the concave lens the refracted ray diverges away from the axis.

mcqs.stem: Which two quantities are needed to calculate the magnification produced by a lens?

options.text: The focal length of the lens and the object height
options.rationale: The focal length describes the lens, but it plays no part in the magnification equation given by the specification.

options.text: The distance to the image and to the object
options.rationale: Distances are measured in ray diagrams, but the specification's equation uses heights, not distances.

options.text: The height of the image and the focal length
options.rationale: This keeps one correct quantity but replaces the object height with a distance that the equation does not use.

options.text: The height of the image and the object height
options.rationale: The specification gives magnification = (image height)/(object height), so the two heights are what is needed.

mcqs.stem: An object 5 mm tall produces an image 15 mm tall. What is the magnification?

options.text: 3, from 15 mm divided by 5 mm
options.rationale: magnification = (image height)/(object height) = 15/5 = 3, written as a plain number.

options.text: 0.33, from 5 mm divided by 15 mm
options.rationale: The fraction has been inverted, dividing the object height by the image height.

options.text: 3 mm, as the heights were in mm
options.rationale: The value is right but the unit is not: dividing mm by mm cancels the unit entirely.

options.text: 10, from 15 mm minus 5 mm
options.rationale: Subtracting gives the extra height, not the number of times larger the image is.

mcqs.stem: An object 8.0 cm tall produces an image 2.4 cm tall. What is the magnification?

options.text: 3.3, since 8.0 is divided by 2.4
options.rationale: The heights have been divided the wrong way round, giving the reciprocal of the magnification.

options.text: 0.30, as the image is smaller
options.rationale: magnification = (image height)/(object height) = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30, a value less than 1 because the image is diminished.

options.text: 3.3, because a lens should enlarge
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of magnify makes an answer below 1 look wrong, so the fraction is turned over.

options.text: 0.30 cm, from the heights in cm
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right, but a ratio of two heights has no unit.

mcqs.stem: A student measures both heights in centimetres and calculates a magnification of 2.5. How should this answer be written?

options.text: As 2.5 cm, keeping the unit of the heights measured
options.rationale: Carrying the starting unit through is the habit here, but cm divided by cm leaves no unit at all.

options.text: As 2.5 mm, since mm is a unit used for heights
options.rationale: This both invents a unit and changes it, when the heights were measured in centimetres anyway.

options.text: As 2.5 m, because metres are the SI unit of length
options.rationale: Converting to the SI unit is a sensible habit for lengths, but a magnification is not a length.

options.text: As 2.5 on its own, because a ratio has no units at all
options.rationale: Magnification is a ratio and so has no units, so the answer is the bare number 2.5.

mcqs.stem: An object is 4.0 cm tall and its image is 60 mm tall. What must be done before the magnification equation is used?

options.text: Convert one height so that both are in the same unit
options.rationale: Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm; here 4.0 cm becomes 40 mm, giving a magnification of 1.5.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a magnification has no unit anyway
options.rationale: The unit only cancels when it is the same top and bottom; dividing 60 mm by 4.0 cm gives 15, not 1.5.

options.text: Divide the two heights just as they are given
options.rationale: Reflects m13: whether one height is in cm and the other in mm does not matter, so the heights are divided without any conversion.

options.text: Divide the larger height by the smaller height
options.rationale: This rule guarantees an answer above 1 and ignores which height is the image height.

mcqs.stem: In ray diagrams, which symbol is used to represent a convex lens?

options.text: A vertical line with two arrowheads pointing inwards
options.rationale: Inward arrowheads are the concave symbol; students choose them because a convex lens brings rays inwards.

options.text: A vertical line with outward arrowheads at each end
options.rationale: The convex lens is drawn as a straight vertical line whose arrowheads point outwards, matching the outward bulge of the lens.

options.text: A shape drawn curved outwards on each of its two faces
options.rationale: That is what the lens really looks like, but ray diagrams use the straight-line symbol instead.

options.text: A vertical line with a single inward arrowhead
options.rationale: Reflects m15: inward arrowheads are taken to signify a convex lens, so an inward-arrowhead symbol is chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol is used in a ray diagram to represent a concave lens?

options.text: A line with arrowheads pointing outwards at both ends
options.rationale: Outward arrowheads represent a convex lens, so this is the other lens symbol.

options.text: A line drawn thinner in the middle than at the edges
options.rationale: That is the true shape of a concave lens, but ray diagrams use the arrowed straight line.

options.text: A line with inward arrowheads at both ends
options.rationale: The concave lens is drawn as a straight vertical line whose arrowheads point inwards, towards the principal axis.

options.text: A line with a single outward arrowhead
options.rationale: Reflects m15: outward arrowheads are taken to signify a concave lens, so an outward-arrowhead symbol is chosen.
